background: The coded phrase is 'Silent Majority.' background: Any scientific paper should show the authors affiliations, who they work for. The author of this paper, Julie Goodman, works for Gradient. Gradient is a business in the US that specializes in hiring scientists to defend their clients products suspected of being toxic. One primary function of these scientists is to produce scientific articles that can be used as evidence to stop government agencies from strengthening public health protections. Often this begins with lawyers identifying strategies that could be used in court, and then Gradient will hire scientists to identify evidence supporting these demands, or, identify weaknesses in the studies that identified the product in question as harmful or carcinogenic. Most of the time, these 'studies' are simply literature reviews that either (a) cherry pick the data that best fits their pre-conceived defense strategy, or (b) determine that the 'weight of evidence is insufficient'. They then publish these results in journals that are industry friendly, like 'Critical Reviews in Toxicology' or 'Environmental Research'. They have hired scientists to defend asbestos, various known pollutants, lead, and just about anything associated with climate change or greenhouse gases.

background: The history of seat belt regulations provides a valuable historical example of governments' attempts to protect their population and the inevitable backlash from those who value personal choice over public health. The first law concerning seat belt regulations in the USA passed in 1968 and required manufacturers to install seat belts in new cars. In the 1970s the government passed additional laws requiring manufacturers to provide other safety mechanisms such as seat belt interlocking mechanisms or passive restraints (such as air bags). This changed in 1980, when Ronald Reagan was elected as president. He ran his campaign on deregulation and so he suspended some of these requirements. However, the insurance industry, which was financially responsible for the safety of car passengers, sued the Reagan administration in 1983 for removing these requirements. The case went to the Supreme court where they ruled unanimously in favor of the insurers and ordered the Department of Transportation to reinstate the requirement(s). In 1985, New York was the first state to require the use of seat belts. During the next few years there was a strong public education campaign and rates of acceptance gradually increased, and today, well over 90% of people regularly wear their seat belts. The arguments against seat belt laws during this time were very reminiscent of arguments against many laws and regulations in discussion today, in that they were largely about personal choice or personal responsibility. Other arguments were more focused on fears that seat belts might actually be dangerous and could lead to strangling or difficulty to escape a crashed car.

background: Johnson & Johnson (J&J) sold cosmetic talc products (including Baby Powder) for decades while maintaining that their talc was asbestos-free. Internal documents later revealed this to be false. In the 1970s, J&J assured the FDA that their internal tests found no trace of asbestos in talc. But J&J failed to mentioned that tests from external laboratories found asbestos in its talc during this same period. In 1977, an article was published in the influential medical journal, the Lancet, stating that “there is no reason to believe that normal consumer exposure to cosmetic talc has in the past led either to cancer at any site or to measurable loss of lung function'. On December 8 2025, the Lancet received a letter from Professors David Rosner and Gerald Markowitz, explaining that the published article was written by a paid consultant of J&J. Furthermore, they provided evidence that a draft of this piece was shared by the author with J&J and edited following their feedback. In other words, it was manufactured doubt. As a result, there have been many lawsuits claiming that long-term use of talc products has caused ovarian cancer or mesothelioma, and in some cases J&J was found guilty and ordered to pay billions of dollars in damages.

background: In the summer of 1955, a 14 year old boy from Chicago named Emmett Till was excited to visit his Uncle in Mississippi. Before leaving, Emmett's mother warned him that Mississippi was a different world and instructed him how to behave in front of white people in the South. But young Emmett, like most people outside the South, did not completely understand these differences. While the specific details are not clear, the basic story is that one night Emmett and his cousins were driving around and Emmett entered a store alone and began to flirt with an employee, a white woman named Carolyn Bryant. After it was clear she was not interested, as Emmett was leaving, he supposedly whistled at the young woman. In the South, this broke an unwritten code of behavior for a black man interacting with a white woman. Carolyn was the wife of Roy Bryant. Roy Bryant eventually heard about this from someone else, and it was reported that he assumed that in this town, for him to do nothing would have marked him as a coward or a fool. Some days later, young Emmett Till was abducted from his Uncle’s house at gun point by Roy Bryant and his half brother J.W. Milam. Carolyn was present and helped identify him. That was how Emmett's fate was sealed, just for a whistle. After a call to the Leflore County Sheriff George Smith, Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam were questioned. They admitted to abducting the boy but claimed they released him later. They were arrested for kidnapping. Three days after his abduction, Emmett Till's body was found floating in the Tallahatchie river. Emmett's face was unrecognizable, but he was wearing his father's silver ring with the initials L.T. carved in it. The defense attorneys and the Sheriff of Tallahatchie County, H.C. Strider, claimed that the lynching of Emmett Till was organized by the NAACP and that evidence had been planted to frame the white men. Sheriff Strider, who initially positively identified the body and changed his mind later, claimed the NAACP wanted to embarrass Mississippi. There were multiple eye witnesses including Emmett Till’s uncle who Bryant threatened on the night Emmett was abducted. Two key witnesses, Levi Collins and Henry Lee Loggins were reported to have seen Bryant and Milam in the shed that Emmett was beaten in. But conveniently enough Sheriff Strider booked them into into a Charleston Mississippi jail in order to keep them from testifying. Despite two eye witnesses risking their lives to testify that they saw Bryant and Milam with Emmett, after 5 days, an all white jury acquitted both Bryant and Milam after a short 67-minute deliberation. In November 1955, a grand jury declined to indict Bryant and Milam for kidnapping, despite the fact that they admitted to kidnapping young Emmett. We the public know all of the details of Emmett Till’s murder because Bryant and Milam confessed to the murder after the trial. Just four months after their acquittal, they were offered $4,000 to tell their story, and they accepted. They knew the details of 'Double Jeopardy' in the US which states that nobody can be charged more than twice for the same crime. Bryant and Milam also assumed their story would vindicate them among segregationists but this poetically backfired as the admission of killing an innocent child outraged the general public and became a crucial moment in the civil rights movement. During the fall of 1955, hundreds of thousands of people protested Emmett's murder in Chicago and other large cities. These remarkable protests helped further ignite the civil rights movement. In fact, only a few months later, a woman was so disgusted by this story, she decided to put actions into words by keeping her seat on a Montgomery bus on December 1, 1955. Her name was Rosa Parks. Many protesters in the 1960s identified themselves as the 'Emmett Till generation'.

explanation: The ground truth: oil and gas companies knew plastic recycling was economically unviable but funded recycling campaigns anyway to keep selling plastic. The left post cites the EPA and acknowledges industry investment in recycling infrastructure, but frames the story as a corporate fraud requiring regulatory intervention — omitting that the policy failures were also shaped by municipal and consumer behavior factors, and implying deliberate deception as the sole cause. The right post cites the American Chemistry Council and acknowledges that internal documents are damaging, but pivots to emphasize regulatory overreach as the real problem — minimizing corporate deception by redirecting blame toward government. Both posts reference the same earthhow.com link, which covers reduce-reuse-recycle principles broadly and does support general claims about recycling's limitations, but does not specifically document the industry's internal knowledge or deception campaigns — players who click the link will find partial but not direct support. The neutral post cites a specific documented finding (industry spending on recycling promotion despite internal doubts) without editorialize or assigning a policy remedy, making it the most accurate representation of the ground truth.
background: For years, recycling companies shipped plastic waste to China until China stopped accepting it two years ago, leaving people in the recycling business scrambling for U.S. buyers and finding takers only for certain items. The truth is that most plastic isn't valuable and never has been. Internal documents and interviews with former officials reveal that the oil and gas companies making plastic knew recycling wouldn't work, even as they spent millions telling the public otherwise. 'There is serious doubt that [recycling plastic] can ever be made viable on an economic basis,' one insider wrote in 1974. They pushed recycling anyway because, as former Society of the Plastics Industry president Larry Thomas put it, selling recycling sold plastic: 'If the public thinks that recycling is working, then they are not going to be as concerned about the environment.' The economics are simple. Collecting, sorting, and melting used plastic is expensive, and plastic degrades after just one or two reuses. New plastic, made cheaply from oil and gas, is almost always better and cheaper. So despite decades of effort and industry scientists privately calling recycling 'infeasible' less than 10 percent of plastic has ever been recycled. The recycling centers the industry funded mostly folded within a couple of years. For an industry whose job is to sell as much oil as possible, recycled plastic is just competition for them. Production is now expected to triple by 2050. However, non-plastic materials like metal, glass, and paper recycle extremely well, and in these cases recycling truly saves energy and resources.

The right post employs a different tactic by challenging study methodology, acknowledging previous research but arguing that confounding factors make the results unreliable. background: In 2011, two Italian epidemiologists, Carlo La Vecchia and Paolo Boffetta, were paid by the Italian Montefibre company to testify in a court case where the company was charged with criminal negligence in regard to a number of its employees dying from mesothelioma as a result of exposure to asbestos. Vecchia and Boffetta argued that the employees were exposed during employment at a previous company and the damage was already done. Additional exposures at Montefibre caused no additional harm to their health. While an appeal to the court case was pending, Drs La Vecchia and Boffetta decided to publish a scientific paper that simply repeated most of their court case arguments. They submitted this review paper and four days later, it was published. This suggests that the peer review process, an important part of scientific publications, either did not take place, or met the absolute minimum requirements. It just so happens that Dr La Vecchia is also an Associate Editor for the journal that published the manuscript in such a rushed fashion(European Journal of Cancer Prevention). Interestingly in the article, Drs La Vecchia and Boffetta declared they had 'no conflicts of interest', meaning that they do not gain financially in any way from the results of the study. This was completely false as they were hired and paid by the Montefibre company to make these same arguments in court. They even claimed that the work for the paper was 'conducted with the contribution of the Italian Association for Cancer Research'. Again, this was false, but it did benefit the Montefibre company in their court case. Only on rare occassions do scientists team up to point out flaws in a single published article. In 2014, this is exactly what happened. In a letter to the President of the journal in question, over 140 scientists, doctors, and organizations collaborated to illustrate the seriousness of their flawed science and ethically dubious protocols. They showed that in this review article of the dangers of asbestos, Drs La Vecchia and Boffetta cherry picked the data and omitted prominent articles that didn't support their pre-conceived ideas. It is clear that the article was published because it benefitted the interests of the company that paid them.

background: In the studies linked in these posts, the authors have affiliations to ChemRisk and the American Petroleum Institute. ChemRisk, which was part of Cardno and now Stantec, is a for-profit scientific consulting firm, ie, product defence firm. They were paid to re-analyze a dataset that the company believed would lead to future lawsuits. This method often employed by the product defence industry is known as the ‘re-analysis'. The time between exposure to a toxic chemical and the disease it causes can sometimes take years to decades for symptoms to occur. The studies that discover these associations are complicated and challenging for many reasons. If an industry responsible for producing the suspected toxic chemical re-analyzes the data, they can cherry pick and re-define the entire analysis: how the samples are selected, what statistical analysis is appropriate, what timeframe to examine, all of which can lead to completely different conclusions. Just like with most other product defence strategies funded by the manufacturers themselves, they often coincidentally lead to much looser restrictions. Under President Donald Trump, congressman Lamar Smith introduced legislation for the 'Secret Science Reform Act', which required all data used by the EPA to be open to other researchers. Open data at face value is a good thing, but a mandatory requirement for all research to be open is meant to benefit industry and not the general population. First, many important and large studies cannot release this data because of privacy reasons established before the study was even conducted. Second, more applicable here, is that it allows product defence companies like Gradient, Exponent, TERA, and ChemRisk to re-analyze the data to coincidentally come to conclusions that benefit their funders. These studies can then be used in court cases by the manufacturers to defend themselves.

background: Johnson & Johnson (J&J) sold cosmetic talc products (including Baby Powder) for decades while maintaining that their talc was asbestos-free. Internal documents later revealed this to be false. In the 1970s, J&J assured the FDA that their internal tests found no trace of asbestos in talc. But J&J failed to mentioned that tests from external laboratories found asbestos in its talc during this same period. In 1977, an article was published in the influential medical journal, the Lancet, stating that “there is no reason to believe that normal consumer exposure to cosmetic talc has in the past led either to cancer at any site or to measurable loss of lung function'. On December 8 2025, the Lancet received a letter from Professors David Rosner and Gerald Markowitz, explaining that the published article was written by a paid consultant of J&J. Furthermore, they provided evidence that a draft of this piece was shared by the author with J&J and edited following their feedback. In other words, it was manufactured doubt. As a result, there have been many lawsuits claiming that long-term use of talc products has caused ovarian cancer or mesothelioma, and in some cases J&J was found guilty and ordered to pay billions of dollars in damages.

background: In 2003, Dr Willie Soon and Dr Sallie Baliunas of the Harvard-Smithsonian Centre for Astrophysics, published a study reviewing data from 240 scientific papers in an attempt to find evidence for temperature anomalies, or flaws in the current climate change models. Using this pooled data, Dr Soon and Dr Baliunas concluded that 'the 20th century is probably not the warmest or a uniquely extreme climatic period of the last millennium'. Many of the scientists cited in this review categorically denied these conclusions and were confused how their data had been misrepresented in such a drastic manner. It would later emerge that Willie Soon received over $1.25 million dollars from Exxon Mobile, the American Petroleum Institute, and Southern Company (one of the largest coal burning electric utilities in the US). Over time, a consensus was reached that this paper was fundamentally flawed after many scientists identified methodological flaws and egregious errors in Dr Soon's analysis. As a result, several scientists resigned from the editorial board of the journal responsible for publishing the article. To their credit, after acknowledging that the review process had 'utterly failed' by not identifying the problems of this article prior to its publication, the journal Climate Research changed their system of editing scientific papers in order to ensure these mistakes would not happen again.

Accounts from that time state that some were required to memorize the constitution itself and write it down, word for word. background: Johnson & Johnson (J&J) sold cosmetic talc products (including Baby Powder) for decades while maintaining that their talc was asbestos-free. Internal documents later revealed this to be false. In the 1970s, J&J assured the FDA that their internal tests found no trace of asbestos in talc. But J&J failed to mentioned that tests from external laboratories found asbestos in its talc during this same period. In 1977, an article was published in the influential medical journal, the Lancet, stating that “there is no reason to believe that normal consumer exposure to cosmetic talc has in the past led either to cancer at any site or to measurable loss of lung function'. On December 8 2025, the Lancet received a letter from Professors David Rosner and Gerald Markowitz, explaining that the published article was written by a paid consultant of J&J. Furthermore, they provided evidence that a draft of this piece was shared by the author with J&J and edited following their feedback. In other words, it was manufactured doubt. As a result, there have been many lawsuits claiming that long-term use of talc products has caused ovarian cancer or mesothelioma, and in some cases J&J was found guilty and ordered to pay billions of dollars in damages.

explanation: A candidate is speaking at a school board forum about whether the federal government should have the power to set curriculum standards and control funding for local schools. The debate is over how much authority should rest with local communities versus Washington. Whereas Sam Brown's post explicitly mentions the documented dog whistle phrase 'States Rights', Hana Robinson's post argues the same pro-local-control position using plain descriptive language ('local school boards,' 'community priorities,' 'district decisions') that carries no such history and would not be recognised as a signal by any specific in-group.
background: The coded phrase is 'States' Rights.' While it sounds like a neutral argument about the balance of governmental power, it carries a well-documented history. The phrase was used prominently by Strom Thurmond during his 1948 Dixiecrat presidential campaign, where 'States' Rights' explicitly meant the right of Southern states to maintain racial segregation against federal civil rights mandates. In the 1960s, the same phrase was used by other hard line segregationists like George Wallace. These candidates used the phrase as an argument specifically for segregation. After the civil rights movement however, speaking about segregation became unpopular so instead of mentioning race specifically, politicians like Richard Nixon learned to cut out the comments about race and just use the 'States Rights' phrase (and others like it) in order to silently rekindle this history. Decades later, Ronald Reagan opened his 1980 presidential campaign in Philadelphia, Mississippi — the town where three civil rights workers had been murdered in 1964 — and declared 'I believe in states' rights.' According to a Reagan advisor named Lee Atwater, the choice of location was not accidental. As described in his 1981 interview, the phrase in that setting signalled support for rolling back federal civil rights enforcement, not merely abstract constitutional preference. Atwater explicitly documented in his own words how 'States' Rights' evolved from segregationist language into a legally neutral-sounding framework that could communicate racial resentment without mentioning race. In the context of education policy, invoking 'States' Rights' specifically — rather than 'local control,' 'community input,' or 'district authority' — activates this documented historical signal.

explanation_references.label: Lee Atwater 1981 interview — explicit account of how 'States' Rights' functioned as coded language in the Southern Strategy

background: In 1996, a tobacco attorney named Chris Horner was thinking of methods to weaken government agencies like the EPA. He proposed to construct procedural hurdles the agency must follow in issuing scientific reports. Specifically, he proposed what sounds reasonable, to require the EPA to provide access to the raw data in all studies used to protect the public. But, even from his own words (see below), his goal was not to improve the scientific process, but to disrupt it. This requirement would radically remove the number of studies the EPA could utilize to build an argument for safety regulations. Due to privacy reasons, it is illegal to share data for most studies involving humans. The EPA could redact this information, but, this would cost an additional tens of millions of dollars so it usually is avoided altogether. Under Donald Trump's leadership, Lamar Smith quickly introduced a bill that encapsulated these ideas for legislation, calling it the 'Honest and Open New EPA Science Treatment Act', or, the 'Honest Act'. Donald Trump justified the extra tens of millions of dollars it would cost to redact these studies by simply removing the studies completely and selecting those that could even be considered in the first place. This is a clear attempt to cherry-pick the science that the industry agrees with.

background: In 2003, Dr Willie Soon and Dr Sallie Baliunas of the Harvard-Smithsonian Centre for Astrophysics, published a study reviewing data from 240 scientific papers in an attempt to find evidence for temperature anomalies, or flaws in the current climate change models. Using this pooled data, Dr Soon and Dr Baliunas concluded that 'the 20th century is probably not the warmest or a uniquely extreme climatic period of the last millennium'. Many of the scientists cited in this review categorically denied these conclusions and were confused how their data had been misrepresented in such a drastic manner. It would later emerge that Willie Soon received over $1.25 million dollars from Exxon Mobile, the American Petroleum Institute, and Southern Company (one of the largest coal burning electric utilities in the US). Over time, a consensus was reached that this paper was fundamentally flawed after many scientists identified methodological flaws and egregious errors in Dr Soon's analysis. As a result, several scientists resigned from the editorial board of the journal responsible for publishing the article. To their credit, after acknowledging that the review process had 'utterly failed' by not identifying the problems of this article prior to its publication, the journal Climate Research changed their system of editing scientific papers in order to ensure these mistakes would not happen again.

background: The history of seat belt regulations provides a valuable historical example of governments' attempts to protect their population and the inevitable backlash from those who value personal choice over public health. The first law concerning seat belt regulations in the USA passed in 1968 and required manufacturers to install seat belts in new cars. In the 1970s the government passed additional laws requiring manufacturers to provide other safety mechanisms such as seat belt interlocking mechanisms or passive restraints (such as air bags). This changed in 1980, when Ronald Reagan was elected as president. He ran his campaign on deregulation and so he suspended some of these requirements. However, the insurance industry, which was financially responsible for the safety of car passengers, sued the Reagan administration in 1983 for removing these requirements. The case went to the Supreme court where they ruled unanimously in favor of the insurers and ordered the Department of Transportation to reinstate the requirement(s). In 1985, New York was the first state to require the use of seat belts. During the next few years there was a strong public education campaign and rates of acceptance gradually increased, and today, well over 90% of people regularly wear their seat belts. The arguments against seat belt laws during this time were very reminiscent of arguments against many laws and regulations in discussion today, in that they were largely about personal choice or personal responsibility. Other arguments were more focused on fears that seat belts might actually be dangerous and could lead to strangling or difficulty to escape a crashed car.

explanation_references.label: History of seat belt laws in the USA

background: Dubbed the 'trial of the century,' the 1925 case of State of Tennessee v. John T. The trial concerned the alleged violation of a Tennessee state law that banned the teaching of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by a high-school teacher, John T. Scopes. The trial's proceedings highlighted many of the cultural tensions of American society that still exist today: secularism versus fundamentalism, science versus religious dogma, and modernism versus traditional views.

background: In the summer of 1955, a 14 year old boy from Chicago named Emmett Till was excited to visit his Uncle in Mississippi. Before leaving, Emmett's mother warned him that Mississippi was a different world and instructed him how to behave in front of white people in the South. But young Emmett, like most people outside the South, did not completely understand these differences. While the specific details are not clear, the basic story is that one night Emmett and his cousins were driving around and Emmett entered a store alone and began to flirt with an employee, a white woman named Carolyn Bryant. After it was clear she was not interested, as Emmett was leaving, he supposedly whistled at the young woman. In the South, this broke an unwritten code of behavior for a black man interacting with a white woman. Carolyn was the wife of Roy Bryant. Roy Bryant eventually heard about this from someone else, and it was reported that he assumed that in this town, for him to do nothing would have marked him as a coward or a fool. Some days later, young Emmett Till was abducted from his Uncle’s house at gun point by Roy Bryant and his half brother J.W. Milam. Carolyn was present and helped identify him. That was how Emmett's fate was sealed, just for a whistle. After a call to the Leflore County Sheriff George Smith, Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam were questioned. They admitted to abducting the boy but claimed they released him later. They were arrested for kidnapping. Three days after his abduction, Emmett Till's body was found floating in the Tallahatchie river. Emmett's face was unrecognizable, but he was wearing his father's silver ring with the initials L.T. carved in it. The defense attorneys and the Sheriff of Tallahatchie County, H.C. Strider, claimed that the lynching of Emmett Till was organized by the NAACP and that evidence had been planted to frame the white men. Sheriff Strider, who initially positively identified the body and changed his mind later, claimed the NAACP wanted to embarrass Mississippi. There were multiple eye witnesses including Emmett Till’s uncle who Bryant threatened on the night Emmett was abducted. Two key witnesses, Levi Collins and Henry Lee Loggins were reported to have seen Bryant and Milam in the shed that Emmett was beaten in. But conveniently enough Sheriff Strider booked them into into a Charleston Mississippi jail in order to keep them from testifying. Despite two eye witnesses risking their lives to testify that they saw Bryant and Milam with Emmett, after 5 days, an all white jury acquitted both Bryant and Milam after a short 67-minute deliberation. In November 1955, a grand jury declined to indict Bryant and Milam for kidnapping, despite the fact that they admitted to kidnapping young Emmett. We the public know all of the details of Emmett Till’s murder because Bryant and Milam confessed to the murder after the trial. Just four months after their acquittal, they were offered $4,000 to tell their story, and they accepted. They knew the details of 'Double Jeopardy' in the US which states that nobody can be charged more than twice for the same crime. Bryant and Milam also assumed their story would vindicate them among segregationists but this poetically backfired as the admission of killing an innocent child outraged the general public and became a crucial moment in the civil rights movement. During the fall of 1955, hundreds of thousands of people protested Emmett's murder in Chicago and other large cities. These remarkable protests helped further ignite the civil rights movement. In fact, only a few months later, a woman was so disgusted by this story, she decided to put actions into words by keeping her seat on a Montgomery bus on December 1, 1955. Her name was Rosa Parks. Many protesters in the 1960s identified themselves as the 'Emmett Till generation'.

explanation_terms.definition: An explanation that attributes events to a secret coordinated plot. The tell is unfalsifiability: absence of evidence gets treated as proof of a cover-up.

background: Hydraulic fracturing, or “fracking,” is a method of oil and gas extraction that involves a drilling process where millions of gallons of water, sand, and chemicals under high pressure are injected into underground wells in order to break the rock formations and release the trapped resources. This process can lead to local and ground water contamination, often detected by the local residents themselves due to unusual tastes or smells in their drinking water. Another issue with fracking is the disposal of the wastewater used in this drilling process. Generally regarded as the safest and most cost-efficient method of disposal, the wastewater is injected into wells deep underground. In areas of the US that use this method of extraction and disposal there can be tens of thousands of these wells, each containing up to 4.5 million gallons of contaminated wastewater. In some instances, this disposal method has been found to cause earthquakes. These fracking sites require monitoring by independent scientists and regulators, but this doesn't always go as planned. Over a 4 month period, Texas cities Azle, Reno, and Springtown experienced more than 30 earthquakes. This seismic activity began after the injection of fracking wastewater into deep wells. Luckily the Texas Railroad Commission was there to assist. On the RRC website it states: '(The RRC is) the state's oldest regulatory agency, RRC has had a critical role of protecting the interests of the public, and as long as it exists the commissioners and employees will fiercely defend the public's interests.' However, the commissioners that run the RRC hardly ever disagree with the oil and gas industry and coincidentally has received tens of millions of dollars from them. For example, Ryan Sitton, who has been heavily involved in the RRCs response to the earthquakes, received $700,000 from the oil and gas industry over just a two year period. He has gone so far as to even use their private jets. Even if Ryan Sitton and others at the RRC have honest intentions, one has to ask why these businesses are so willing to pay them every year?

background: In 1999 the FDA approved a new painkiller named Vioxx. In 2000, the drug maker Merck created a study aiming to prove that Vioxx was a more effective alternative compared with older painkillers. This clinical trial had mixed results. Independent studies found it had 2.4 times the risk of cardiovascular events compared with the control, Aleve. Merck researchers argued that these heart attacks were random and that they didn't occur with those taking Aleve because Aleve acts like a low dose aspirin, protecting them from heart attacks. Subsequent clinical trials involving Vioxx were halted because people taking Vioxx again had more heart attacks. Merck even went so far as to pay medical doctors to put their names on flawed scientific publications that supported Vioxx. Eventually, Vioxx was taken off of the market, but a bit too late: the FDA estimated that Vioxx caused between 88,000 and 139,000 heart attacks. Merck pled guilty to a $950 million fine and settled several other lawsuits by paying $5 billion. This story illustrates that studies from industries investigating their own products are often biased and need true independent studies for verification.

background: The coded phrase is 'Urban Youth.' Closely linked to housing development in the USA, 'urban' underwent a documented semantic shift stretching back to the 1930s. Following the Great Depression, the US government implemented the New Deal to help boost the American economy. During the Depression, the construction of new houses was practically non-existent. So, the federal government implemented a public housing construction project. Except this project was not designed for all of the general public. From 1934 - 1968, a practice known as 'Redlining' was used, where sections of cities were divided based specifically on race. Black neighborhoods were treated differently as they were determined to be a financial risk under the assumption that their presence, even a single family, lowered property values. The organization in charge of this project, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), provided financial support to housing developers as long as they only sold to white families and they would not provide loans to home buyers looking to buy in these 'flagged' neighborhoods. If a Black family bought a home in a white neighborhood, the FHA downgraded the neighborhood using color-coded risk maps under the rationale that 'incompatible racial groups should not be permitted to live in the same community' as it caused 'instability'. Since it was determined to be a financial hazard, any white homebuyer attempting to buy in a mixed neighborhood was blocked from getting an FHA-backed loan. White families were further encouraged to move into new suburban developments through reduced mortgages that were sometimes cheaper than rent. These policies and financial incentives encouraged white families to leave cities, an event known as the 'white flight'. These changes systematically drained cities of their economic base due to the loss of tax revenue. Prior to 'white flight' and redlining, the phrases 'urban' and 'inner city' referred to primarily a geographic term. However, they quickly changed into a racialized socioeconomic code word used by certain politicians and segments of the media as a replacement for Black and Latino communities. In the media, 'urban' was most often paired with negative terms such as 'urban decay' and 'urban crisis' signifying poverty, crime, and government dependency. Redlining and other legalized forms of prejudiced real estate practices were later declared illegal by the Fair Housing Act in 1968.

explanation: A school board is holding a public hearing on tightening eligibility rules for the district's subsidized lunch program after costs rose. Community members and local officials are weighing in on who truly qualifies for assistance and whether the current system is being abused. While the phrase 'welfare queen' is used in Kevin Sullivan's post, Sean Clark's uses plain administrative language — 'eligibility requirements,' 'verify household income,' 'limited resources' — that describes the same budget concern without invoking any historically coded figure or stereotype. A reader unfamiliar with the term's history would have no reason to flag Clark's post as anything other than ordinary civic commentary.
background: The coded phrase is 'Welfare Queen'. The term was popularized by Ronald Reagan during his 1976 and 1980 presidential campaigns, where he repeatedly told the story of a Chicago woman who had defrauded the welfare system — driving a Cadillac and living lavishly on public funds. Reagan never explicitly named her race, but the image he conjured was understood by a broad audience to depict a Black woman, because American media had for years overwhelmingly depicted welfare recipients as Black (by 1973, roughly 75% of magazine images of welfare recipients featured Black Americans, even though Black Americans made up only about 35% of recipients). The phrase therefore signals, to an audience steeped in that media history, a lazy, fraudulent urban Black woman exploiting taxpayer money — carrying a racial charge that Reagan could deny while the audience received it. Applying 'Welfare Queen' to a school lunch hearing activates the same imagery: it implies that the families using the program are fraudsters gaming the system at others' expense, coded by race.

background: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest serving First Lady from 1933 - 1945. explanation: A state legislature is debating whether public universities must include a mandatory humanities survey course in general education requirements. Supporters and critics are submitting written testimony about what such a course should emphasize. The plain post (Catherine Foster) argues for broad, rigorous humanities requirements using straightforward language about historical literacy, critical thinking, and civic preparation — none of which carry that documented secondary meaning. A reader unfamiliar with the coded usage would find both posts equally plausible advocacy; the difference lies entirely in the phrase Andrea Reed chose.
background: The coded phrase is 'Western Civilization.' Academically the term is legitimate — the Greek, Roman, and European historical and philosophical traditions — though even there it is a recent construct, the phrase was created during the First World War to explain to American soldiers why they were fighting in Europe. In online political discourse and white nationalist communities it has been co-opted as a code phrase for white racial identity, and is particularly attractive to believers in the 'Great Replacement,' the conspiracy theory that white populations are being deliberately displaced by non-white immigrants. In these contexts the phrase typically signals demographic replacement framing (immigrants will 'destroy' it), civilizational-threat framing (other cultures are 'incompatible' with it), or cultural purity framing (integration requirements should enforce conformity). Similar framing appeared in the manifestos behind the Christchurch, El Paso, and Buffalo attacks. On a 2016 MSNBC panel, Iowa Congressman Steve King claimed no 'subgroup of people' had contributed more to civilization than white people; challenged afterwards, he said he had meant Western civilization, adding that much of it happens to be Caucasian. There is nothing wrong saying that Western civilization has produced enormous and influential achievements. And it is also historically true that many of the people who produced those achievements were Europeans, or what would now be called 'white'. King took the step of suggesting that the accomplishments of Western civilization provide evidence for the superiority of the racial group associated with it. But the history of the West didn't start from scratch: it was built up from advancements made in previous civilizations. Furthermore, advancements in the West weren't produced by a single ethnic group. Greeks, Romans, Germanic peoples, Celts, Jews, Arabs and Muslims, Byzantines, Slavs, Iberians, Africans, and many others participated in the intellectual and cultural history that eventually gets categorized as “Western.” When people imply that white people today share the intelligence and creativity of ancient civilizations simply because of their race, they are at best oversimplifying human history and culture and at worst misunderstanding the relevance of skin color. Claiming superiority because you share a basic skin color with leaders from a distant past is like calling a beige house cat a lion because they happen to be the same color.

background: In 1996, a tobacco attorney named Chris Horner was thinking of methods to weaken government agencies like the EPA. He proposed to construct procedural hurdles the agency must follow in issuing scientific reports. Specifically, he proposed what sounds reasonable, to require the EPA to provide access to the raw data in all studies used to protect the public. But, even from his own words (see below), his goal was not to improve the scientific process, but to disrupt it. This requirement would radically remove the number of studies the EPA could utilize to build an argument for safety regulations. Due to privacy reasons, it is illegal to share data for most studies involving humans. The EPA could redact this information, but, this would cost an additional tens of millions of dollars so it usually is avoided altogether. Under Donald Trump's leadership, Lamar Smith quickly introduced a bill that encapsulated these ideas for legislation, calling it the 'Honest and Open New EPA Science Treatment Act', or, the 'Honest Act'. Donald Trump justified the extra tens of millions of dollars it would cost to redact these studies by simply removing the studies completely and selecting those that could even be considered in the first place. This is a clear attempt to cherry-pick the science that the industry agrees with.

explanation: A school board in a mid-sized district is holding a public meeting to review proposed changes to its social studies curriculum. Parents, teachers, and local officials have shown up to weigh in on what students should learn about American history. Invoking 'Critical Race Theory' as in the post by Catherine Yamada, signals to a certain audience that any honest treatment of race in American history is ideological indoctrination; to a general audience, it sounds like a specific and reasonable objection to a new school curriculum. The plain post by Thomas Young objects to the same curriculum changes using direct, non-coded language — 'what students are taught about race and American history' — which describes the actual subject of debate without activating the specific political signal.
background: The coded phrase is 'Critical Race Theory' (CRT). CRT is a graduate-level scholarly and legal framework, developed in the 1970s–80s by Kimberlé Crenshaw and Derrick Bell, that examines how laws and institutions can perpetuate racial inequality. It originally had nothing to do with K–12 curricula, only with individual graduate-level law school classes. Beginning around 2020–2021, Republican politicians and conservative media figures — including Christopher Rufo, who explicitly stated publicly — that they would deliberately broaden the term far beyond its original academic meaning. Rufo openly stated in a 2021 tweet that his goal was to 'capture' the phrase and redefine it to encompass virtually any classroom discussion of racism, slavery, redlining, or systemic inequality in American history. Rufo essentially manufactured a culture war by weaponizing the term. He stated openly that his goal was to rebrand it as toxic, to have the public immediately think CRT and dismiss the argument outright - whenever they read progressive ideas about race and culture.

explanation: The left post uses 'insufficient evidence' framing to dismiss cancer risks at low benzene concentrations, while acknowledging EPA concerns but minimizing them. The right post challenges study methodology and shifts focus to occupational vs. environmental exposure, dismissing broader cancer links. Both posts cite the same study but cherry-pick different conclusions to manufacture doubt about benzene's dangers. The neutral post simply reports new research findings without editorial spin. All three use identical professional tone, making bias detectable only through structure and emphasis rather than emotional language. None of the posts mention the authors clear associations to product defence industries and companies with products associated with benzene.
background: In the studies linked in these posts, the authors have affiliations to ChemRisk and the American Petroleum Institute. ChemRisk, which was part of Cardno and now Stantec, is a for-profit scientific consulting firm, ie, product defence firm. They were paid to re-analyze a dataset that the company believed would lead to future lawsuits. This method often employed by the product defence industry is known as the ‘re-analysis'. The time between exposure to a toxic chemical and the disease it causes can sometimes take years to decades for symptoms to occur. The studies that discover these associations are complicated and challenging for many reasons. If an industry responsible for producing the suspected toxic chemical re-analyzes the data, they can cherry pick and re-define the entire analysis: how the samples are selected, what statistical analysis is appropriate, what timeframe to examine, all of which can lead to completely different conclusions. Just like with most other product defence strategies funded by the manufacturers themselves, they often coincidentally lead to much looser restrictions. Under President Donald Trump, congressman Lamar Smith introduced legislation for the 'Secret Science Reform Act', which required all data used by the EPA to be open to other researchers. Open data at face value is a good thing, but a mandatory requirement for all research to be open is meant to benefit industry and not the general population. First, many important and large studies cannot release this data because of privacy reasons established before the study was even conducted. Second, more applicable here, is that it allows product defence companies like Gradient, Exponent, TERA, and ChemRisk to re-analyze the data to coincidentally come to conclusions that benefit their funders. These studies can then be used in court cases by the manufacturers to defend themselves.

Because of the wage cap (~$168,600–$176,100 in recent years), Musk's Social Security contribution maxes out at roughly the same level as someone earning around $184,500. He pays NO additional Social Security tax on his billions above that cap. Beyond the false claim, the post's surface signals are classic Level 1 red flags: the 'author' is a brand-style name ('Liberty Truth Network') rather than a real outlet, the handle has a slogan and year (@FreedomTruth_USA_1776), and the reference URL mimics a real domain but belongs to a sketchy site — all signs to catch BEFORE you even read the post body.
background: America's wealthiest 400 families own 2-3% of all US wealth, as much as the bottom 60% of the population (~190 million people). When it comes to their income, proportionally the top 1% pay a higher tax rate, 26%, compared to the middle class (~8-13%). But when you realize that the majority of their wealth (on average over 56%) is from unrealized gains (stocks etc), which are not taxed at all, then proportionally they pay roughly 8.2% tax in a given year. This is proportionally less tax paid than the average middle class family. Some reports have found many actually pay closer to just 3.4%. When it comes to Social Security tax, as of 2026 the federal government taxes 6.2% of your wages — but only up to $184,500. Here's the benefit for the ultra-rich: they likely don't earn wages. Most of their money comes from capital gains, which isn't subject to Social Security tax at all. So a trillionaire whose wealth is purely in stocks could pay $0 in Social Security tax — while a nurse or teacher pays 6.2% on every dollar they earn. At most, a trillionaire pays the same Social Security tax as someone earning $184,500 — and only if they happen to draw that much in actual wages.

background: The coded phrase is 'Non-British.' In UK crime reporting, selectively flagging a suspect's nationality or national origin only when they are assumed to be from a minority or immigrant background — while omitting such details for white British suspects — is a documented strategy to signal ethnic or racial 'otherness' without stating it directly. The phrase 'non-British' (or 'non-national') has been documented by press watchdogs and media researchers as a framing device that implies immigrant or ethnic-minority identity is associated with criminal behaviour. It communicates to an audience already primed by anti-immigration discourse that the suspect's foreignness is the salient fact — not the alleged conduct. The UK's Independent Press Standards Organisation and academic media analysts have flagged exactly this pattern: nationality is newsworthy when the suspect reads as 'other,' and invisible when they do not.

explanation: A suburban school board is debating a federal court order requiring students to be transported to schools outside their immediate neighborhoods in order to integrate the district. Community members are speaking out on both sides. Tessa Howard's post uses the phrase verbatim and purposely or not, activating the dog whistle for a certain audience. David Saito's post covers the same debate — federal court orders, school assignment, neighborhood boundaries — using plain descriptive language ('court-ordered school assignment policy,' 'students being reassigned') that carries no documented coded history and does not signal opposition to integration to any particular in-group.
background: The coded phrase is 'Forced Busing.' On its surface it sounds like a neutral description of a government transportation program, but it carries a well-documented racial subtext rooted in the politics of the late 1960s and 1970s. In the decade following the 1954 Supreme Court decision (Brown v. Board of Education) declaring segregation to be unconstitutional, most schools remained racially segregated. Initially, parents were given the Freedom of Choice to choose which schools their children could attend. However, most schools remained segregated as only a small minority of black students chose to attend a predominantly white school and close to zero white students chose to attend a predominantly black school. States that had racism and segregation engrained into their social structures and cultures attempted to bypass these laws by opening private schools for white children only, many with the support of the Citizen's Council. In one case in Prince Edward County, Virginia, the government chose to defund public schools entirely rather than segregate. White children were instead provided funding to attend private schools while black children, with no private schools in their neighborhoods, were left with no choice for education. In Boston, school district lines were drawn intentionally to racially segregate the schools. Due to many other examples of avoiding segregation, another Supreme Court decision (Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education) ruled that federal courts could use busing as an integration tool. Not surprisingly, this was not that popular in racially segregated cultures. Politicians understood these sentiments and began using the phrase 'Forced busing' as a dog whistle when discussions of race became socially unacceptable. As Lee Atwater explained in his anonymously recorded 1981 interview detailing the Republican 'Southern Strategy,' 'Forced Busing' was one of a set of abstract policy phrases deliberately adopted to appeal to white voters' anxieties about school integration without mentioning race directly. Richard Nixon used the phrase prominently during his 1968 presidential campaign to signal opposition to federal court orders requiring that Black and white students attend the same schools — orders that were the direct legal remedy for decades of state-enforced segregation. To the target audience, 'Forced Busing' communicated opposition to racial integration while remaining deniable as mere concern for local control, parental choice, or government overreach. The word 'forced' does specific work: it frames the federal integration mandate as coercive tyranny rather than a constitutional remedy, and it invites the listener to identify the government — not the segregated school system — as the aggressor.

explanation: Both biased posts cherry-pick data from the same regulatory report to manufacture doubt about fracking risks. The left post uses 'insufficient evidence' framing while citing regulatory gaps, omitting that these gaps don't prove safety. But it does acknowledge that more independent research is needed. The right post however implies that the Energy Institute is independent. This is a stretch considering that the institute receives millions of dollars from the oil and gas industry. Furthermore, the right post shifts blame to pre-existing contamination, citing baseline data while omitting evidence of fracking-related increases. Both reference the same source but highlight different sections. The neutral post reports the actual study findings without hedging or blame-shifting. However, the neutral post fails to identify any conflicts of interest. All three posts appear equally authoritative and data-driven, making the bias subtle and harder to detect.
background: Hydraulic fracturing, or “fracking,” is a method of oil and gas extraction that involves a drilling process where millions of gallons of water, sand, and chemicals under high pressure are injected into underground wells in order to break the rock formations and release the trapped resources. This process can lead to local and ground water contamination, often detected by the local residents themselves due to unusual tastes or smells in their drinking water. Another issue with fracking is the disposal of the wastewater used in this drilling process. Generally regarded as the safest and most cost-efficient method of disposal, the wastewater is injected into wells deep underground. In areas of the US that use this method of extraction and disposal there can be tens of thousands of these wells, each containing up to 4.5 million gallons of contaminated wastewater. In some instances, this disposal method has been found to cause earthquakes. These fracking sites require monitoring by independent scientists and regulators, but this doesn't always go as planned. The linked article in these posts concerns one such report from the University of Texas (UT) in 2012 that claimed there was no link between fracking and water contamination. Later that year, the Public Accountability Initiative reported that the head of the study, UT professor Dr. Charles “Chip” Groat, was on the board of an oil drilling company for the duration of the study and was paid over $1.5 million dollars over the course of 5 years. This was a clear conflict of interest that he failed to disclose. UT then called for an independent review which found many errors and flaws with how the study was conducted and published. Dr. Groat retired in the wake of this controversy.

background: Hydraulic fracturing, or “fracking,” is a method of oil and gas extraction that involves a drilling process where millions of gallons of water, sand, and chemicals under high pressure are injected into underground wells in order to break the rock formations and release the trapped resources. This process can lead to local and ground water contamination, often detected by the local residents themselves due to unusual tastes or smells in their drinking water. Another issue with fracking is the disposal of the wastewater used in this drilling process. Generally regarded as the safest and most cost-efficient method of disposal, the wastewater is injected into wells deep underground. In areas of the US that use this method of extraction and disposal there can be tens of thousands of these wells, each containing up to 4.5 million gallons of contaminated wastewater. In some instances, this disposal method has been found to cause earthquakes. These fracking sites require monitoring by independent scientists and regulators, but this doesn't always go as planned. Over a 4 month period, Texas cities Azle, Reno, and Springtown experienced more than 30 earthquakes. This seismic activity began after the injection of fracking wastewater into deep wells. Luckily the Texas Railroad Commission was there to assist. On the RRC website it states: '(The RRC is) the state's oldest regulatory agency, RRC has had a critical role of protecting the interests of the public, and as long as it exists the commissioners and employees will fiercely defend the public's interests.' background: Hydraulic fracturing, or “fracking,” is a method of oil and gas extraction that involves a drilling process where millions of gallons of water, sand, and chemicals under high pressure are injected into underground wells in order to break the rock formations and release the trapped resources. This process can lead to local and ground water contamination, often detected by the local residents themselves due to unusual tastes or smells in their drinking water. Another issue with fracking is the disposal of the wastewater used in this drilling process. Generally regarded as the safest and most cost-efficient method of disposal, the wastewater is injected into wells deep underground. In areas of the US that use this method of extraction and disposal there can be tens of thousands of these wells, each containing up to 4.5 million gallons of contaminated wastewater. In some instances, this disposal method has been found to cause earthquakes. These fracking sites require monitoring by independent scientists and regulators, but this doesn't always go as planned. The linked article in these posts concerns one such report from the University of Texas (UT) in 2012 that claimed there was no link between fracking and water contamination. Later that year, the Public Accountability Initiative reported that the head of the study, UT professor Dr. Charles “Chip” Groat, was on the board of an oil drilling company for the duration of the study and was paid over $1.5 million dollars over the course of 5 years. This was a clear conflict of interest that he failed to disclose. UT then called for an independent review which found many errors and flaws with how the study was conducted and published. Dr. Groat retired in the wake of this controversy.

background: It is important that scientists and public figures follow the facts in order to limit speculation that can be used as misinformation and conspiracy theories. Science builds upon itself by following the best available evidence and always maintains an open mind since the next experiment might challenge prevailing assumptions. The origins of the SARS-CoV-2 virus responsible for COVID-19 is still very contentious within certain social media circles. Among scientists however, it is widely accepted that SARS-CoV-2 arose from a zoonotic event because virtually all available data suppors it. Similar zoonotic events have happened dozens of times over the last century. SARS-CoV-2 is not the first virus thought to have arisen from a laboratory: there are many who believe that HIV and Ebola viruses were also designed in a laboratory. Ironically for Ebola, many of the rumors were very similar to SARS-Cov-2 in that a research laboratory was in close proximity to the outbreak and it was supposedly designed to be a bioweapon. But, these rumors are now mostly whispers because of other unrelated outbreaks as well as the diversity of related viruses recovered from surrounding wildlife populations that are likely the true precursors. We cannot progress as a society when evidence-based hypotheses are equated with rumors. Especially those rumors spread by people who benefit by spreading them.

background: Segregation was the systematic separation of people based on racial categorizations in the United States.
